sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces the chapter's coverage of pre-paving construction items -- grade control and acceptance, concrete plant operation inspection, and paving equipment inspection -- and lists the critical readiness checks that should be completed before production paving starts.
sections.body: This chapter discusses pre-paving construction items, including grade control and acceptance, concrete plant operation inspection, and paving equipment inspection. Addressing these items early may help avoid problems associated with concrete quality, pavement thickness, and concrete placement and finishing operations. The following critical elements should be in place before production paving starts: check all equipment in the paving train to ensure it is operational; verify that an acceptable length of grade is available for concrete paving; check that approved test reports are available for all materials in storage at the job site and the plant site; verify that backup testing equipment is available and develop extra equipment backup plans; verify that all necessary concrete placement tools are available (hand tools, straightedges, hand floats, edgers, hand vibrators); verify that extra vibrators and joint-sawing equipment are available in case original equipment breaks down; verify that radio/telephone communication with the plant is operational; verify that equipment is available to water the grade if necessary; monitor the string line regularly and re-tension as necessary; verify that the day's work header is in place; develop an extreme weather management plan; check the weather forecast for each day of paving; ensure a sufficient length of plastic covering is available in case of sudden rain; and verify positive drainage within the plant site.
key_points: Chapter covers pre-paving items: grade control and acceptance, concrete plant operation inspection, and paving equipment inspection.
Verify all paving-train equipment is operational and an acceptable grade length is available before production paving.
Confirm approved material test reports are on hand and backup testing equipment/plans exist.
Confirm placement tools, extra vibrators, and joint-sawing equipment are available for breakdowns.
Confirm radio/telephone plant communication and grade-watering equipment are operational.
Monitor/re-tension the string line and confirm the day's work header is in place.
Develop an extreme weather plan, check the daily forecast, and stage plastic covering for sudden rain.
Verify positive drainage within the plant site.
sections.applicability: Applies as a pre-paving readiness checklist before production concrete paving begins.

sections.title: Grade Acceptance
sections.summary: Covers acceptance of the base grade after placement, trimming, leveling, and compaction, including checking elevation tolerances against plans, the cost and thickness-variability consequences of a low or variable final grade, removing loose debris before paving, and the importance of grade control to construction drainage and pavement service life.
sections.body: The grade is accepted after the base layer is placed, trimmed, leveled, and compacted. Proper base grade ensures that nominal pavement thickness is achieved and final profiles and elevations are consistent with contract documents. Elevation tolerances for each pavement layer must be checked, as elevations and tolerances are shown on plans for the compacted subgrade, stabilized and non-stabilized layers, and top of pavement. Prior to paving, consider the effect of grade on as-placed concrete volume and the materials cost impact if the final grade is low; the effect of grade on pavement thickness variability, since a variable final grade affects thickness determined through core sampling and can affect payment for thickness (minimize concrete thickness variability accordingly); and remove loose debris from the base before paving. Proper base grade control is critical, as it affects drainage during construction and the service life of the pavement.
key_points: Grade is accepted after the base layer is placed, trimmed, leveled, and compacted, and must match contract elevations/profiles.
Check elevation tolerances for each layer (subgrade, stabilized/non-stabilized layers, top of pavement) against the plans.
A low final grade increases as-placed concrete volume and materials cost.
A variable final grade increases pavement thickness variability, which affects core-sampled thickness and potentially payment.
Remove loose debris from the base before paving.
Proper base grade control affects both construction drainage and long-term pavement service life.
sections.applicability: Applies when accepting the finished base grade prior to concrete paving.

sections.title: Concrete Plant Operation
sections.summary: Frames concrete as a manufactured product sensitive to quality-control variation during manufacture, requiring the plant to be in good condition, operate reliably, and produce acceptable concrete uniformly batch to batch; detailed requirements are developed in the child subsections.
sections.body: Concrete is a manufactured product, whose quality and uniformity are sensitive to quality control variation during manufacture. A plant must be in good condition, operate reliably, and produce acceptable concrete uniformly from batch to batch.
key_points: Concrete quality and uniformity are sensitive to quality-control variation during manufacture.
The plant must be in good condition, operate reliably, and produce acceptable concrete uniformly batch to batch.
Detailed plant requirements are covered in the child subsections: quality/uniformity, pre-production inspection, traffic flow, stockpile management, and uniformity testing.
sections.applicability: Applies as the organizing heading for concrete batch plant operation requirements (sections 6-3.1 through 6-3.5).

sections.title: Quality and Uniformity
sections.summary: Attributes concrete quality/uniformity problems chiefly to aggregate segregation and varying aggregate moisture content, and lists the ASTM C94/CRD-C 31 batch plant requirements: separate aggregate bins with precise shutoff, hopper-charging monitoring, scale accuracy of +/-0.2 percent, and dosing accuracy tolerances for cement/water, aggregate, and admixture.
sections.body: Concrete quality and uniformity are greatly affected by aggregate segregation and varying moisture content of the aggregates. Batch plants and equipment must meet ASTM C94/CRD-C 31. Key items listed in ASTM C94/CRD-C 31 for batch plants are: separate aggregate bins for each size of coarse aggregate with the capability of shutting off material with precision; controls to monitor aggregate quantities during hopper charging; scales accurate to +/- 0.2 percent, tested within each quarter of the total scale capacity, with adequate standard test weights available for checking scale accuracy; cement and water added to an accuracy of +/- 1 percent of the required total mass; aggregate added to an accuracy of +/- 2 percent of the required total mass; and admixture added to an accuracy of +/- 3 percent of the required total mass.
key_points: Concrete quality/uniformity is greatly affected by aggregate segregation and varying aggregate moisture content.
Batch plants and equipment must meet ASTM C94/CRD-C 31.
Separate aggregate bins per coarse aggregate size, with precise shutoff capability and hopper-charging monitoring controls.
Scale accuracy: +/- 0.2 percent, tested within each quarter of total scale capacity, with standard test weights available.
Cement and water dosing accuracy: +/- 1 percent of required total mass.
Aggregate dosing accuracy: +/- 2 percent of required total mass.
Admixture dosing accuracy: +/- 3 percent of required total mass.
sections.applicability: Applies to the design and operation of batch plant equipment used to produce concrete for paving.

sections.title: Pre-production Inspection
sections.summary: Requires the engineer to inspect the concrete plant before paving starts (and whenever uniformity or strength problems occur) using the NRMCA certification checklist, and lists the specific items to inspect: stockpile drainage/separation, bin partitions, scales, water meter, lines, boilers/chillers, admixture dispensers, mixers, hauling units, material certifications, and batching operations.
sections.body: The engineer should inspect the concrete plant before the start of paving using the National Ready Mixed Concrete Association (NRMCA) checklist in Certification of Ready Mixed Concrete Production Facilities. Plants should be inspected before the start (or re-start) of each paving project and when uniformity or strength problems are encountered during production. The inspection should include: checking foundations of stockpiles for proper separation and adequate drainage; checking bins for adequate partitions to prevent intermingling of aggregates; checking scales with test weights throughout the range to be used and for seals by an approved agency; checking the water meter for accuracy and checking for leakage of lines; checking the capacity of boilers and chillers if their use is anticipated; checking admixture dispensers for accuracy; checking mixers for hardened concrete around blades and inspecting concrete hauling units for cleanliness; ensuring all concrete-making materials have been certified and approved for use; observing stockpiling and bin-charging operations to verify segregation and contamination will not occur; reviewing aggregate moisture tests; observing batching operations at start and periodically during production; and checking scales for zeroing and confirming proper batch weights are set on the scales.
key_points: Engineer inspects the plant before paving starts (and on re-start, or when uniformity/strength problems occur) using the NRMCA checklist.
Check stockpile foundation drainage/separation and bin partitions to prevent aggregate intermingling.
Check scales with test weights across the full use range, and confirm scale seals by an approved agency.
Check water meter accuracy, line leakage, and boiler/chiller capacity if used; check admixture dispenser accuracy.
Check mixers for hardened concrete buildup and hauling units for cleanliness; confirm materials are certified/approved.
Observe stockpiling and bin-charging for segregation/contamination, and review aggregate moisture test records.
Observe batching operations at start and periodically during production; check scale zeroing and batch weight settings.
sections.applicability: Applies before paving begins (or restarts) and whenever concrete uniformity or strength issues arise during production, to verify plant readiness.

sections.title: Traffic Flow
sections.summary: Calls for optimizing plant traffic flow, considering raw material delivery, concrete delivery to the paver, CQC/QA-related traffic and testing personnel safety, aggregate stockpile equipment operation, and general plant safety requirements.
sections.body: Optimize the traffic flow at the plant. Consider the delivery of raw materials; the delivery of concrete to the paver; CQC/QA-related traffic operations and testing personnel safety; the operation of equipment for managing the aggregate stockpiles; and plant safety requirements.
key_points: Optimize plant traffic flow across raw material delivery and concrete delivery to the paver.
Account for CQC/QA-related traffic operations and testing personnel safety.
Coordinate equipment operation for managing aggregate stockpiles within the traffic pattern.
Address overall plant safety requirements as part of traffic flow planning.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning vehicle and equipment traffic patterns at a concrete batch plant serving a paving project.

sections.title: Managing the Aggregate Stockpile
sections.summary: Requires developed stockpile management procedures addressing storage pads, unloading, stockpile heights, bin charging, and moisture, and lists nine key practices covering handling to minimize segregation/degradation, moisture monitoring, drop-height limits, stockpile separation, bulldozer restrictions, and contamination prevention.
sections.body: Develop and implement stockpile management procedures. Procedures must address construction of stockpile storage pads, keeping loader buckets off the floor, truck unloading, maximum stockpile heights, bin charging, quality control sampling, water sprinkling, aggregate washing, and aggregate moistures. Key items include: handle and store aggregates to minimize segregation and degradation and prevent contamination by deleterious substances; closely monitor and maintain aggregate stockpiles to keep moisture content at or above saturated surface dry condition, particularly important for absorptive aggregates in hot weather; if aggregate moisture varies through the day, increase the frequency of moisture determination (variability increases when loaders retrieve from one area of a stockpile or sprinkling is not uniform); adjust water added at the mixer for aggregate moisture, considering chilled water in hot weather; limit the aggregate drop height when building a stockpile, building it up in uniform-thickness layers, and remove material vertically from bottom to top so each load contains a portion of each layer; keep stockpiles separated from one another, using a wall if there is not enough space to keep size fractions separate; do not allow bulldozers on stockpiles, since they break down aggregate and segregate particle sizes; reduce contamination (from clay/mud tracked in by trucks, from stockpiling by end loaders instead of belt placers, and from loaders scraping the bottom of the pile when charging bins) by stabilizing haul roads and dump areas; and visually examine stockpiles for segregation, performing gradation testing from representative areas if apparent and rejecting segregated material.
key_points: Develop stockpile procedures covering storage pads, unloading, maximum heights, bin charging, QC sampling, sprinkling, washing, and moisture.
Handle/store aggregates to minimize segregation and degradation and prevent contamination.
Maintain stockpile moisture at or above saturated surface dry (SSD), especially for absorptive aggregates in hot weather; test more often if moisture varies during the day.
Adjust mixer water for aggregate moisture; consider chilled water in hot weather.
Limit stockpile drop height, build in uniform layers, and remove material vertically bottom-to-top.
Keep stockpiles separated (use a dividing wall if space is limited) and never allow bulldozers on stockpiles.
Prevent contamination from tracked-in clay/mud, end-loader stockpiling, and bin-charging pile scraping; stabilize haul roads and dump areas.
Visually inspect for segregation, confirm with gradation testing, and reject segregated material.
sections.applicability: Applies to the handling, storage, and quality control of aggregate stockpiles at the concrete batch plant.

sections.title: Concrete Uniformity Testing
sections.summary: Requires concrete uniformity testing before paving starts to establish minimum mixing times, comparing samples taken at 15 and 85 percent drum discharge against ASTM C94 allowable differences (5 of 6 tests), with stationary plants tested per CRD-C 55, and lists the six required uniformity test parameters.
sections.body: Conduct concrete uniformity testing before the start of paving; uniformity testing establishes minimum mixing times. Truck mixers must meet ASTM C94/CRD-C 31. Uniformity tests compare differences in concrete sampled at approximately 15 percent and 85 percent drum discharge; differences between concrete discharged at 15 and 85 percent should be less than the maximum allowable differences stated in ASTM C94 for five of six tests. Test batch (stationary) plants in accordance with CRD-C 55, which differs from ASTM C94 in that it requires three samples from an individual batch. Minimum mixing times for production are established by the concrete uniformity tests. The six tests required for each method are: density (unit weight); air content; slump; coarse aggregate content; air-free mortar unit weight; and seven-day concrete compressive strength.
key_points: Conduct concrete uniformity testing before paving starts; it establishes minimum production mixing times.
Truck mixers must meet ASTM C94/CRD-C 31.
Compare samples at ~15% and 85% drum discharge; differences must be less than ASTM C94 maximum allowable for 5 of 6 tests.
Stationary (batch) plants are tested per CRD-C 55, which requires three samples from an individual batch (differs from ASTM C94).
Six required uniformity tests: density (unit weight), air content, slump, coarse aggregate content, air-free mortar unit weight, and seven-day compressive strength.
sections.applicability: Applies before production paving begins, to establish and verify minimum concrete mixing times via uniformity testing.

sections.title: Paving Equipment Issues
sections.summary: Lists pre-paving equipment checks: availability of required equipment and backups, proper working order of haulers/placers/spreaders/pavers/curing rigs/saws, slipform paver vibrator frequency/amplitude requirements per CRD-C 521, curing application equipment, and joint-saw blade suitability for the aggregate type.
sections.body: Check the paving equipment for the following: availability of required pieces of equipment (for example, the number of trucks hauling concrete affects slipform production rates), with extra equipment such as concrete saws onsite in case of mechanical breakdown; that equipment is in proper working order, including concrete haulers, concrete placers, concrete spreaders, slipform pavers, curing/texture rigs, and sawcutting equipment; that slipform pavers achieve proper consolidation through vibration, checking vibrator frequency and amplitude prior to paving -- spud vibrators under no load must have a frequency of no less than 135 Hz (8,000 vibrations per minute) and an amplitude of 0.75 mm (0.03 in.) as determined in CRD-C 521, while tube vibrators under no load must have a frequency of no less than 80 Hz (5,000 vibrations per minute) and an amplitude of 0.75 mm (0.03 in.), with vibrator elevations established so they do not interfere with pre-placed dowel baskets; that curing application equipment ensures uniform and proper application of curing compound; and that blades for joint sawing are suitable for the aggregate type used in the mix.
key_points: Verify availability of required paving-train equipment (e.g., haul truck count affects slipform production rate) and extra equipment (e.g., saws) for breakdowns.
Verify proper working order of haulers, placers, spreaders, slipform pavers, curing/texture rigs, and sawcutting equipment.
Spud vibrators (no load): frequency >= 135 Hz (8,000 vpm), amplitude 0.75 mm (0.03 in.), per CRD-C 521.
Tube vibrators (no load): frequency >= 80 Hz (5,000 vpm), amplitude 0.75 mm (0.03 in.).
Set vibrator elevations to avoid interfering with pre-placed dowel baskets.
Verify curing application equipment achieves uniform, proper curing compound application.
Joint-saw blades must be suitable for the aggregate type used in the concrete mix.
sections.applicability: Applies to pre-paving inspection of hauling, placing, slipform, curing, and joint-sawing equipment before production paving begins.

sections.title: Stringline Issues
sections.summary: Explains that stringline elevation and offset accuracy governs the alignment and elevation control of grade trimming, subbase/base placement, and the paving train, and therefore the final pavement smoothness; describes stake interval guidance (7.6 m/25 ft on tangents) with tighter spacing on vertical curves.
sections.body: The accuracy of the elevations and offset distances for grade reference points is important to the final smoothness of the pavement surface. These elevations and offsets provide the basis for establishing the stringline, which provides an accurate reference for elevation and alignment control of the grade trimming, subbase/base placement, and concrete paving train. The final product reflects any error in the stringline. Setting up the stringline takes careful planning; the interval between stakes is important, particularly on vertical curves. On tangent sections, a maximum staking interval of 7.6 m (25 ft) will usually result in a good product. A tighter interval is necessary to produce smooth pavements on vertical curves, based on the rate of change of curvature.
key_points: Stringline accuracy (elevations and offsets at grade reference points) directly governs final pavement smoothness.
The stringline provides elevation/alignment control for grade trimming, subbase/base placement, and the paving train; errors carry through to the final product.
On tangent sections, a maximum staking interval of 7.6 m (25 ft) usually produces a good result.
Tighter stake intervals are required on vertical curves, scaled to the rate of change of curvature.
sections.applicability: Applies when establishing the stringline system used to control grade trimming, base placement, and concrete paving alignment.

sections.title: Stringline Aids
sections.summary: Lists seven practical aids for establishing and maintaining a proper stringline: using rigid stakes and quality line, avoiding knots and splices, preventing sag, checking for staking errors, and monitoring/adjusting the line as conditions require.
sections.body: The following aid in establishing a proper stringline: use rigid stakes; use quality line; avoid knots and splices; prevent perceptible sagging; eyeball for staking errors and irregularities; monitor, protect, and maintain the line; and adjust stake spacing to fit conditions.
key_points: Use rigid stakes and quality line.
Avoid knots and splices in the stringline.
Prevent perceptible sagging of the line.
Visually check (eyeball) for staking errors and irregularities.
Monitor, protect, and maintain the stringline throughout use.
Adjust stake spacing to fit site conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies to field crews setting up and maintaining a stringline for grade and paving alignment control.

sections.title: Stringline Type
sections.summary: Compares two stringline materials: braided nylon (polyester/Kevlar/polyethylene) line, typically 3 mm (1/8 in.) diameter, lightweight with good pull strength but prone to sag and stretch requiring frequent monitoring; and aircraft cable, typically 2.5 mm (3/32 in.) galvanized cable, with less sag, less weather sensitivity, and less stretch over time, at the cost of more difficult splicing.
sections.body: Stringline materials and their properties and behaviors are as follows. Braided nylon (polyester, Kevlar, polyethylene) line is typically 3 mm (1/8 in.) diameter braided string; it is lightweight but has good pull strength, does not crimp like wire, and does not result in hand injury (cuts), but it develops a sag, stretches over time, and requires frequent monitoring. Aircraft cable is typically 2.5 mm (3/32 in.) galvanized cable; splicing is not as simple as with nylon string, but it exhibits less sag, is less affected by weather (humidity), and stretches less over time.
key_points: Braided nylon line (polyester/Kevlar/polyethylene) is typically 3 mm (1/8 in.) diameter, lightweight with good pull strength.
Nylon line does not crimp like wire and does not cause hand injury, but develops sag and stretches over time, requiring frequent monitoring.
Aircraft cable is typically 2.5 mm (3/32 in.) galvanized cable.
Aircraft cable has less sag, is less affected by weather/humidity, and stretches less over time than nylon line, but splicing is more difficult.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting stringline material (braided nylon versus aircraft cable) for grade and paving alignment control.
